**February 29, 1960 — a Monday**

You were born on a day that doesn't exist in three out of every four years. That's where we have to start.

**The rarest birthday in the calendar:** February 29 occurs only in leap years, which means the calendar has granted you a true birthday — the actual date, not an adjacent substitute — only 16 times in your 66 years of life. You marked your 15th real February 29 in 2020, during the first weeks of a global pandemic. Your 16th was 2024. The next is 2028, when you'll be 68. Most people accumulate birthdays annually without thinking about them; yours require a year divisible by four.

**The exact day — Agadir disappears:** In the early hours of February 29, 1960, a magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck directly beneath the Moroccan city of Agadir. Because it was shallow and centered under a densely populated area, it killed an estimated 12,000 people — roughly a third of the city's population — in seconds. Agadir was essentially erased and had to be rebuilt from the ground up. The earthquake was relatively modest by seismic measures; the destruction was a lesson in how geology, construction quality, and geography converge to determine what survives. The world received that lesson the day you arrived in it.

**Twenty-eight days before your birth — Greensboro:** On February 1, 1960, four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, ordered coffee, and refused to leave when denied service. By February 29, the sit-in movement they sparked had spread to dozens of cities across the South. The student-led phase of the Civil Rights Movement — more confrontational, less patient than what came before — was in full acceleration the week you were born. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee would be founded six weeks later. You entered a country in the middle of being forced to reckon with itself.

**Three weeks after your birth — Sharpeville:** On March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on Black protesters in Sharpeville, killing 69 people. The massacre transformed international understanding of apartheid and hardened opposition to it globally. You were three weeks old. The struggle against apartheid that began making international headlines around your birth would not end until Nelson Mandela walked free in 1990, when you were 30.

**The year itself is a threshold:** 1960 is the last year of the Eisenhower era — a moment of surface prosperity and deep turbulence. In November, the United States would elect its youngest-ever president, John F. Kennedy, by the thinnest margin in decades. The 1950s, with their enforced consensus and nuclear-family mythology, were ending. The decade you were born into would become the most culturally convulsive in modern American history. You grew up inside it.

**The arc of your 66 years:** You were 3 when Kennedy was shot in Dallas. You were 8 during 1968 — King, Robert Kennedy, Chicago — old enough to sense catastrophe but not quite old enough to name it. You were 9 when humans walked on the moon. You came of age under Nixon, Watergate, and the end of Vietnam. You were 20 when Reagan was elected, reshaping the political vocabulary for the next generation. You were 29 when the Berlin Wall fell and the Cold War dissolved faster than anyone had dared predict. You were 41 on September 11, 2001.

**What the calendar gave you:** Every person born in February 1960 came into a world at a particular moment of fracture and possibility. You came into it on the one day that comes and goes unremarked most years — a built-in reminder that time doesn't flow as evenly as the calendar suggests. The world has changed more in your 66 years than in any equivalent span in recorded history, and you've had, by the strict arithmetic of leap years, fewer birthdays to mark it than anyone else born that month.
